title: Estimate how much storage this system needs over 5 years
summary: Tests whether you can size one record correctly, multiply by volume and time, and sanity-check the result against something you already know.

slides.markdown:
"Estimate how much storage this system needs over 5 years" catches two very different failure modes: showing up with **no method at all** (guessing a number), and showing up with a method that produces a **wildly wrong result** because a sanity check was skipped.

The strong answer sizes one record, multiplies it out across volume and time, and then checks the final number against something concrete — a known disk size, a familiar scale — before presenting it as final.

Pin down three inputs before multiplying anything: **size per record** (a message, a row, a document — in bytes), **write rate** (records created per day), and **retention period** (how long data is kept before it's deleted or archived, since "5 years" in the prompt might not mean all of it stays hot the whole time).

If the interviewer doesn't volunteer a record size, propose one out loud and justify it — a chat message's text plus metadata is a very different size than a video file's manifest.

The core formula: **bytes/record × records/day × 365 × years**, then multiply by a **replication factor** for durability — raw data size is never the number you provision against, since production data is always stored on more than one copy.

Say this skeleton out loud before plugging in numbers, the same way you would for a QPS estimate — it's the same discipline of "formula first, numbers second" applied to a different resource. See [storage estimation](storage-estimation) for the deeper mechanics of sizing storage from write volume.

Take a chat message system: 500 bytes per message (text plus metadata), 1 billion messages sent per day.

```
500 bytes/message x 1,000,000,000 messages/day
= 500,000,000,000 bytes/day
= 500 GB/day (raw)
```

Half a terabyte a day is the raw write volume before any multiplication across time or replication — keep this number visible, since every later step just scales it.

Scale the daily figure across 5 years (1,825 days), then apply a 3x replication factor for durability:

```
500 GB/day x 365 days x 5 years = 912,500 GB = 912.5 TB (raw, 5yr)
912.5 TB x 3 (replication) ~= 2,737.5 TB ~= 2.74 PB
```

Replication isn't optional padding — losing the only copy of production data on a single disk failure is unacceptable at any real scale, so the 3x belongs in the estimate from the start, not as an afterthought.

slides.sectionTitle: Walking it: metadata and index overhead
slides.markdown:
Raw data times replication still understates the real footprint. Add **20-30% for metadata and index overhead** — timestamps, foreign keys, search indexes, and the database's own bookkeeping all take real disk space on top of the payload itself.

Applying 25%: 2,737.5 TB × 1.25 ≈ **3,421.9 TB ≈ 3.42 PB**. This is the number you'd actually present as the 5-year storage estimate — every earlier figure was an intermediate step toward it.

slides.sectionTitle: Walking it: converting to a familiar unit and sanity-checking
slides.markdown:
3.42 PB means little on its own — convert it to something you can reason about. At roughly 1TB per consumer drive, that's about **3,420 drives' worth of data**, or, spread across servers holding 20TB of disk each, about **171 servers** of raw storage.

Saying that number out loud is the sanity check itself: if 171 servers of storage sounds absurd for the size of company in the prompt, revisit an input; if it sounds plausible, you've earned the right to present 3.42 PB with confidence.

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: keeping everything hot vs tiering to cold storage
slides.markdown:
**Keeping all 3.42 PB on hot, fast storage** is simple to reason about and to query, but it's the most expensive option by far — hot storage costs several times more per gigabyte than cold. **Tiering** — moving data older than, say, 90 days to cheaper cold storage — cuts cost substantially, since most reads skew toward recent data, but it adds real retrieval latency (minutes, not milliseconds) for anything pulled back from the cold tier.

Name the trade-off explicitly rather than picking one silently: most production systems tier, because the cost savings on rarely-accessed old data dwarfs the occasional slow retrieval.

slides.sectionTitle: Follow-up: how would you reduce this if it's too expensive?
slides.markdown:
Three concrete levers, not vague cost-cutting: a **TTL** that deletes data past its useful life (do chat messages really need to live forever?); **cold storage tiers** for data that's rarely read but must be retained for compliance; and **compression**, which on text-heavy data like chat messages can often cut storage 50-70% with negligible CPU cost.

Naming all three, and which applies here, shows you understand storage cost as a design lever, not a fixed bill you just accept.

slides.sectionTitle: Follow-up: what if attachments or media get added later?
slides.markdown:
"Does this estimate change if the product adds attachments or media later?" — yes, dramatically, and you should say by how much: a single photo can be 200-500x the size of a 500-byte text message, so if even 5% of messages later carry a photo attachment, the media alone could eclipse the entire text-message storage estimate.

The strong answer flags that media storage deserves its own separate estimate with its own record size, rather than folding it into the same formula with the text-message assumptions.

**Wrong belief:** the raw data size (912.5 TB over 5 years) is the number to present.

**Why it's wrong:** production data is never stored as a single copy — losing the only replica to one disk failure is not an acceptable outcome at any real scale. Skipping the replication factor understates the true footprint by roughly 3x, and understates cost by the same margin.

**Correct model:** replication is part of the estimate, not an afterthought — apply it (and the metadata overhead) before presenting a final number.

Compressed script: "At 500 bytes per message and 1 billion messages a day, that's 500GB of raw data daily, or about 912.5TB over 5 years. Applying a 3x replication factor and 25% for metadata and indexes gets us to roughly 3.4 petabytes. That's about 3,400 drives' worth of data, which feels plausible for a system at this scale — I'd tier data older than 90 days to cold storage to control cost."

Practice delivering this fluently — the sanity check at the end is what separates a senior answer from a junior one.
